opus-5.5.text:
I think the expectations are a little ahead of where things actually are, but the direction is real.

Models like Strawberry are genuinely good at reasoning through a well-defined problem: give one a clear spec, a self-contained function, a competitive-programming-style task, and it can do remarkably well, sometimes better than most humans. But that's not what most programming work looks like day to day. Real engineering is messy. You have a huge codebase with years of history, implicit conventions, weird hacks that exist for reasons nobody wrote down, and requirements that change halfway through. A lot of the job is figuring out *what* to build and *why*, not just typing out the implementation.

So "cleaning up code" is a good example. Refactoring sounds mechanical, but to do it well you have to understand the intent of the original author, what's load-bearing and what's accidental, and what the team will want to maintain later. Current models can help a lot with local cleanups, renaming, small restructurings, writing tests. But a deep refactor across a large system still needs someone who holds the whole picture in their head and takes responsibility for the result.

From my own experience writing infrastructure code, the biggest gain is productivity, not replacement. The boring parts, boilerplate, glue code, first drafts, looking up some API you've forgotten, get much faster. That frees you to spend more time on design and debugging the hard stuff. The people who benefit most are those who already know what good code looks like, because they can quickly judge whether the model's output is right.

Long term, yes, I think the bar will keep moving. The tasks models handle reliably will get bigger, from a function, to a module, to maybe a whole feature. Programmers will spend less time writing code line by line and more time specifying, reviewing, and architecting. So the role changes. But "rapidly replace programmers" in the next year or two? I don't think so. It's more like everyone gets a very capable junior collaborator who works incredibly fast, and you still need to be the one who knows where you're going.

r001.rationale: The response says current models can help with local cleanups but deep refactors still need human oversight; it does not state that spaghetti code remained despite expectations that Strawberry would clean it up.

r002.rationale: The response describes change unfolding over time: model tasks will grow from functions to modules and features, programmers’ roles will shift, and rapid replacement in the next year or two is unlikely.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people are getting ahead of themselves. I work on these systems every day, and what I see is that models like Strawberry are genuinely good at a narrow slice of what programmers do: writing a function from a clear spec, translating between languages, filling in boilerplate, explaining a stack trace. That slice is real and it's getting bigger. But it's not the job.

The job is figuring out what to build, understanding why the existing system is shaped the way it is, deciding which tradeoffs are acceptable, and knowing when the thing that looks fine is actually wrong. Those parts require context the model doesn't have, and often context nobody has written down anywhere. When people say the AI will "clean up your code," I ask: clean it up according to what? The model doesn't know that this ugly function is ugly because of a production incident two years ago, or that the "obvious" refactor breaks a client nobody remembers.

So my view is: it will change what programming feels like a lot faster than it changes who is needed. The typing part shrinks. The reviewing, specifying, and verifying part grows, and honestly that part is harder. If you can't read code critically, a very fast code generator is dangerous, not helpful.

I'd also say the benchmarks that drive these headlines reward solving well-posed problems in isolation. Real engineering is almost never well-posed. We should be excited, use the tools aggressively, but the "replace programmers next year" narrative mostly comes from people who aren't maintaining large codebases.

r001.rationale: The response questions what “clean up your code” means, but does not say that spaghetti code remained despite expectations about Strawberry.

r002.rationale: The response says AI will change programming quickly and that the typing part will shrink; it does not characterize the change as slow or gradual.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to separate helping programmers from replacing them. Writing code is only part of the job. You also have to understand what someone wants, decide what tradeoffs to make, and check whether the system actually solves the problem.

With something like Strawberry, I’d want to see how it handles those responsibilities before assuming it will replace programmers rapidly. Cleaning up code sounds simpler, but even there, cleaner-looking code isn’t necessarily correct code. Can it preserve the behavior? Can we verify the changes?

So I’m open to substantial progress. I just think the expectations should follow what these systems can reliably do, rather than what an impressive demonstration suggests.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to separate writing code from doing software engineering. A system might be very good at generating a function or cleaning up a piece of code, but that doesn’t automatically mean it understands what you’re trying to build, why a decision was made, or which tradeoffs matter.

So I’m cautious about claims that something like Strawberry will rapidly replace programmers. It could change their work substantially. But even “cleaning up” code requires judgment: cleaner according to what criteria, and how do you know the behavior hasn’t changed? The important question is how much responsibility the system can reliably take on, and how much checking people still need to do.
